title: Who Holds Power
theme: Civics and government: systems of authority
objectives: I can name and compare monarchies and republics using ten civics words.
I can explain what a legislature, a policy, and a treaty do.
I can use words such as sovereign, oppress, liberty, and reform to describe how power is used and limited.
I can write a short explanation of how a government balances power and freedom.
rationale: Seventh-grade social studies compares systems of government. Three exact terms (monarchy, republic, legislature) are paired with the verbs and nouns that history texts use to argue about them (govern, sovereign, oppress, liberty, reform, policy, treaty). The words are grouped by question: who holds power, how power is used, and how freedom and change push back on power. Bipartisan, unanimous, and regulate come back from earlier units so that students can describe how a legislature actually votes and works. The passage uses a few well-documented facts (the Magna Carta, the structure of Congress, the Treaty of Paris of 1783) so that students practice reading informational text with real dates.

words.def: A system of government in which a king or queen rules, usually for life.
words.ex: In a monarchy, the crown usually passes from a parent to a child.
words.ex2: Spain is a monarchy today, but its king shares power with an elected parliament.
words.nonExample: A country where citizens vote for a president every four years is a republic, not a monarchy.

passage.title: Who Rules? Three Ways to Hold Power
paras: Every society must answer a basic question: who has the power to make decisions for everyone? For much of history, the answer was a monarchy, a system in which a king or queen rules and the title passes through a family. Many monarchs claimed to be sovereign, meaning that no one had greater authority than they did. They could collect taxes, make laws, and declare wars, and ordinary people had little choice but to obey.

Unlimited power often meant that people were oppressed, treated harshly and denied basic rights. In 1215, English nobles forced King John to accept the Magna Carta, a charter that placed limits on what a king could do. It did not create democracy, but it planted a lasting idea: even a ruler must follow the law.

Another way to govern is a republic, in which citizens elect representatives to make decisions on their behalf. In the United States, the Constitution created a republic with a legislature called Congress, which writes the nation's laws. Congress has two parts, the Senate and the House of Representatives, and both must approve a bill before it can become a law.

Leaders in a republic also shape policy, the plan or course of action a government chooses to follow. Policy can cover almost anything, from how roads are built to how schools are funded to what a nation says to other countries. When nations make a formal written agreement with each other, it is called a treaty. After the American Revolution, the Treaty of Paris of 1783 recognized the United States as an independent country.

No government stays exactly the same. Citizens may call for reform, a change that aims to fix problems in a system without throwing the whole system out. Over time, some monarchies have shared power with elected lawmakers, and some republics have widened who is allowed to vote. Each change reflects an effort to protect liberty, the freedom of people to make their own choices, while still allowing a government to govern for the common good.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten civics words, read an informational passage on monarchies, republics, and the limits placed on power, then compare governments using a shared set of terms. The discussion prompts invite more than one viewpoint, and teachers should keep the tone neutral and focus on how the words are used, not on current party politics.

notes.va.monarchy.n: A tier 3 term worth a quick map and timeline. Students may think a monarch always has total power; contrast an absolute monarchy with one that shares power with a parliament. Keep monarchy (the system) and monarch (the person) separate.
notes.va.republic.n: Students often mix up a republic with the Republican party. Show both uses and name which one the unit means. A one-sentence definition on the board: citizens elect leaders to govern for them.
notes.va.legislature.n: Tie to the three branches. Use the family words legislate, legislation, and legislator on a chart. Ask students which part of government hears trials (courts) and which carries out laws (executive) to keep the roles apart.
notes.va.govern.v: The verb is the base for government and governor; show -ment as a suffix that makes a noun. Use sentences with different subjects (a mayor, a council, a student club) to widen the sense.
notes.va.liberty.n: An abstract word; anchor it in specific liberties students can name (speech, religion, assembly). Ask where one person's liberty ends. Keep the conversation open and respectful.
notes.va.oppress.v: A serious word; use historical examples with care and let students respond in writing before discussion. Distinguish oppress from simply being strict: oppression uses power to keep people down unfairly.
notes.va.reform.n: Multiple meaning: reform as a noun (a change that improves) versus the verb for a person who changes bad habits. Contrast reform with revolution using the shades ladder.
notes.va.policy.n: Students often confuse policy with police and with a single rule. Use a school policy students know, such as attendance, to show how it guides many decisions.
notes.va.treaty.n: Stress that a treaty is between countries. Use the Treaty of Paris of 1783 in the passage as one real example, and ask what each side gained.
notes.va.sovereign.adj: Pair with the noun sovereignty. Ask what it would mean for a nation to be self-ruling, and what it might give up by signing a treaty. The word can also name a ruler; keep to the adjective here.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'The passage says many monarchs claimed to be sovereign, meaning no one had greater authority. If no one is above them, then nobody can stop them from passing harsh laws. That is why the next paragraph talks about people being oppressed and about limits like the Magna Carta.'

Fact claims in the passage and examples: Magna Carta sealed by King John in 1215; Congress has two parts that must both approve a bill; Treaty of Paris of 1783 recognized U.S. independence; Spain is a parliamentary monarchy; Rome became a republic after kings and chose officials called consuls. Confirm against a reference.
Sense boundary: sovereign is taught as an adjective only; the noun (a ruler) is not taught. Republic is distinguished from the political party name in the teacher note.
